passages.happening:
‘Thus King Darius ordered a search of the archives stored in the treasury of Babylon’ (verse 1). ‘And a scroll was found in the fortress of Ecbatana, in the province of Media’ (verse 2). On it is a memorandum.

In his first year, it says, King Cyrus issued a decree about the house of God in Jerusalem: ‘Let the house be rebuilt as a place for offering sacrifices, and let its foundations be firmly laid’ (verse 3). It gives the size of the building and the way it is to be built, ‘with three layers of cut stones and one of timbers. The costs are to be paid from the royal treasury’ (verse 4). And the gold and silver articles that Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple ‘must also be returned to the temple in Jerusalem and deposited in the house of God’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The search begins in Babylon, but the scroll turns up far away, in Ecbatana, modern Hamadan in western Iran. Ecbatana was the old capital of Media and a summer residence of the Persian kings. Cyrus is known to have spent time there, so it is a likely place for a record from his first year to be kept.

The memorandum reads like an archive note, not a public announcement. It gives measurements, building methods and funding from the royal treasury, and it orders the return of the vessels. It is plainer than the proclamation of chapter 1, but it says the same thing. The king had given his word, and his word was on file.

A first hearer would feel the turn of the story. In chapter 4 a search of the royal records had stopped the work. Now a search of the royal records sets it free.
passages.later: The memorandum's words, let its foundations be laid, echo the word Isaiah gives the LORD about the temple, in the same breath in which he names Cyrus: ‘Let its foundation be laid’ (Isaiah 44:28).
passages.asks: A forgotten scroll in a distant archive settled the matter. Ask whether you have given up on something good because the proof seemed lost. And ask how you might keep working while you wait for the answer to arrive.

passages.t: Darius's decree: leave the work alone, and pay for it
passages.happening:
Darius writes to Tattenai and his officials. ‘Leave this work on the house of God alone. Let the governor and elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its original site’ (verse 7).

More than that, the cost ‘is to be paid in full to these men from the royal treasury out of the taxes of the provinces west of the Euphrates, so that the work will not be hindered’ (verse 8). The priests in Jerusalem are to be given what they need for the sacrifices every day: bulls, rams and lambs, wheat, salt, wine and oil (verse 9). ‘Then they will be able to offer sacrifices of a sweet aroma to the God of heaven and to pray for the lives of the king and his sons’ (verse 10).

The king threatens anyone who interferes with a cruel public death and the ruin of his house (verse 11). And he ends, ‘May God, who has caused His Name to dwell there, overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to alter this decree or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued the decree. Let it be carried out with diligence’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The inquiry meant to check the builders ends with the governor who questioned them ordered to pay for their work. That is the surprise of the chapter.

The decree fits what is known of Darius. Persian kings supported the temples of their subject peoples. The request for prayers for the king and his sons matches Persian practice too: the Cyrus Cylinder likewise asks the gods Cyrus restored to pray daily for him and his son.

The decree echoes the words of Tattenai's letter, and the phrase the house of God beats through the chapter like a drum.

And notice how Darius speaks of the temple: God ‘has caused His Name to dwell there’ (verse 12). It is the language Israel's own law used for the place God would choose. The decree speaks in words the Jews themselves would use.
passages.later:
The law of Moses had spoken of the place where ‘the LORD your God will choose a dwelling for His Name’ (Deuteronomy 12:11).

Centuries later, Paul asked the churches to pray in the same way that Darius asked of the priests: ‘for kings and all those in authority’ (1 Timothy 2:2).
passages.hard:
What should a reader make of the threat in verse 11?

Darius threatens a cruel public death for anyone who interferes with the decree, and the ruin of his house. His own inscription at Behistun, carved on a cliff in western Iran, boasts of punishing rebels in the same way, so the threat was meant seriously.

The book records the decree of a Persian king. It does not say that God commanded the threat, and it does not hold it up as a model. Its interest is in what God did through the king: the work was protected, and the temple was finished. Nothing in this decree gives anyone today a warrant to threaten or harm anyone, for the sake of a house of God or for any other cause.
passages.asks: A pagan king asked for prayers for his life, and the book records it without embarrassment. Ask whether you pray for those who govern you, including those who do not share your faith. And ask where you have seen God at work through the decisions of people who do not know him.

passages.t: The house is finished and dedicated
passages.happening:
Tattenai and his associates carry out the king's decree with care (verse 13). ‘So the Jewish elders built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo’ (verse 14). They finish ‘according to the command of the God of Israel and the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, kings of Persia’ (verse 14).

‘And this temple was completed on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius’ (verse 15).

The priests, the Levites and the rest of the exiles ‘celebrated the dedication of the house of God with joy’ (verse 16). They offer a hundred bulls, two hundred rams and four hundred lambs, and a sin offering of twelve male goats, ‘one for each tribe of Israel’ (verse 17). And they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their groups ‘according to what is written in the Book of Moses’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Adar is the twelfth month, in February and March. The third of Adar in Darius's sixth year falls early in 515 BC, though some count 516. The house of God stands again about twenty-three years after the first return, and about seventy years after Solomon's temple was burned.

Notice the order in verse 14. God's command comes first, then the kings' decrees. Artaxerxes is named although he reigned later, from 465 to 424 BC; the writer probably includes him because his support for the temple is told in chapter 7.

The offerings are modest compared with Solomon's dedication, where they ran to tens of thousands of animals. That is a reminder of how small and poor the community was. The twelve goats, one for each tribe, show that the returnees, though they came mostly from Judah and Benjamin, saw themselves as standing for the whole people of Israel.

The word for dedication here is the Aramaic chanukkah. The same word in Hebrew names the dedication of the altar in the wilderness and of Solomon's temple, and it later gave its name to Hanukkah, the feast that remembers this same temple's rededication in 164 BC, after the Seleucid king Antiochus IV had desecrated it.

One thing the chapter does not report. When Solomon's temple was dedicated, a cloud filled the house. Here there are sacrifices, priests and great joy, and no cloud.
passages.later:
Solomon's dedication was on a different scale: ‘And Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep’ (1 Kings 8:63). And at Solomon's temple, ‘the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD’ (1 Kings 8:11).

In the year the work began again, Zechariah heard the angel of the LORD ask how long God would withhold mercy from Jerusalem, ‘with which You have been angry these seventy years’ (Zechariah 1:12).

The feast that later remembered this temple's rededication is the ‘Feast of Dedication’ John names in his Gospel (John 10:22).
passages.asks: The house was smaller than the first, and it was finished with joy. Ask whether you can celebrate what God has given even when it is less than what you remember or hoped for. And ask what in your life was finished only because others prayed, spoke up and helped.

passages.happening:
‘On the fourteenth day of the first month, the exiles kept the Passover’ (verse 19). The priests and Levites have purified themselves, and the Levites slaughter the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their brothers the priests, and for themselves (verse 20).

‘The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, together with all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel’ (verse 21).

‘For seven days they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful and turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them to strengthen their hands in the work on the house of the God of Israel’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
At verse 19 the book returns from Aramaic to Hebrew for the Passover.

The Passover, kept on the fourteenth day of the first month, remembered the night God spared Israel's firstborn and brought them out of Egypt. It was followed by the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread. Only those who were ritually clean could eat it, so the priests and Levites purified themselves first. Keeping the Passover just after the temple was finished presents the return from Babylon as a second exodus, another rescue from bondage.

Verse 21 matters. With the returned exiles at the meal were ‘all who had separated themselves from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land’ (verse 21). This was the law's old provision for outsiders who committed themselves to Israel's God. The community's boundary was faith in the LORD, not birth alone. The verb for separate, badal, is the verb of Genesis 1, where God separates light from darkness. It will come back in chapters 9 and 10.

And the king who helped them is called ‘the king of Assyria’ (verse 22). The Persian king now ruled the old Assyrian lands. The empire that had first scattered Israel was, in a sense, helping to restore it.
passages.later:
The law made room for outsiders at the Passover: ‘If a foreigner resides with you and wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all the males in the household must be circumcised; then he may come near to celebrate it, and he shall be like a native of the land’ (Exodus 12:48).

And the wisdom of Proverbs says the same as verse 22: ‘The king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD; He directs it where He pleases’ (Proverbs 21:1).
passages.asks: The table was open to those who turned to seek the LORD. Ask how your church's table looks to someone turning toward God from outside. And ask what joy you have been given lately, and whether you have thanked the God who gave it.
